thread.title: SoftBank: Price Is What You Pay, Asset Supported Value And A Free Option Is What You Get - Part III - SoftBank Group ADR (OTCMKTS:SFTBY)

author: Gordon Investing
title: SoftBank: Price Is What You Pay, Asset Supported Value And A Free Option Is What You Get - Part III - SoftBank Group ADR (OTCMKTS:SFTBY)
text:
Note: Due to SoftBank's ( OTCPK:SFTBY ) complexity and SA article length requirements, there are 4 parts to this write-up: Part I - Executive summary, SoftBank's history, Masayoshi Son's bio and track record . Part II - SoftBank's organizational structure and main holdings. Part III - The Vision Fund and ride-sharing investments. Part IV - Debt, risk, intrinsic value, and conclusion.
For the readers who would prefer to see it all at once, you can go to my blog and read all four parts as a whole.
The Vision Fund: $17b - $88b In 2017, Masa created the Vision Fund, a venture capital behemoth towering in capital over everyone else in Silicon Valley or outside. The fund's committed capital is $97.7b. As a comparison, all of Venture Funds in the US and Europe together raised $42b in 2017.
The goal of the fund is to invest in late-stage tech companies in the areas such as AI, IoT, on-demand economy, ride sharing, robotics, mobile apps, fintech, and connectivity. This interview with a couple of Vision Fund's principles describes in a lot of detail the structure and workings of the Vision Fund and is used to put together many of the details in this part of my analysis.
Although the fund acts like a venture capital vehicle, it is actually set up as private equity, meaning that SoftBank is a manager compensated via management fees calculated as a percentage of assets as well as performance fees that take part of the overall return. The Vision Fund thus does not fit a typical private equity mold. A private equity company usually takes a controlling position in a company, PEs often change management team, while cash flow of the investment is critical due to the need to service high debt load. The Vision Fund does not follow any of that approach. The fund's lifetime is 14 (12+ 2 extension) years, meaning that SoftBank can afford a long-term view without needing to rush for exit via an IPO in order to meet requirements for the Vision Fund investors. The Vision Fund brings to the table not just capital but also connections into an extensive ecosystem of startups and companies SoftBank is affiliated with as well as specific knowledge that can help companies grow.
Before we delve into details, I think it is important to be a little more precise about this fund than what the headline stories portray. Masa did not actually raise $97.7b. In order to get outside investors, Masa had to commit $32.5b of SoftBank's own cash and holdings in various investments. Outside committed capital is closer to $65b, with $60b coming from the Middle East sovereign funds of Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates.
The graph below shows a good general breakdown of the Vision Fund investors.
Source: Financial Times
The Vision Fund is managed by approximately 90 people from the offices in Tokyo, London, and San Carlos, CA. Roughly 50% of invested funds is in the US-based companies, with the other 50% is outside of the US. Target companies are in late-stage growth, and the Vision Fund takes up significant minority stakes, usually between 20% and 35%.
The table below shows the latest list of companies the Vision Fund invested in, from SoftBank's Sept. 30, 2018, Consolidated Financial Report:
There are some important competitive advantages that Masa and SoftBank have vis-a-vis other venture or PE funds:
SoftBank/Vision Fund size and Masa's reputation position them as the first number to call and preferred choice by the up and coming companies hungry for capital. If a founder wants to go big, the Vision Fund is a sensible choice. This is important when it comes to tech. During the early stages, it is not uncommon that a tech concept may have multiple competitors, all trying to do the same thing. Sometimes the differentiator between a winner takes all and the ones that will have to close the shop is simply the amount of capital that each company has at its disposal. That capital can be used on hiring better personnel, investing in more aggressive marketing, or rapidly expanding user and customer base. Although he has a team of people, Masa has a knack for making quick decisions with his investments . This will inevitably lead to some mistakes, but he is spreading his bets, investing in more established companies and later financing rounds, as opposed to the outfits with a few employees as he might have done in the past. He gives founders even more money than they ask if he can challenge them to accelerate their vision and grow quicker. This has been a constant theme in Masa's approach, he often wants founders to go faster and bigger. Long-term approach. Masa's investment horizon is in decades, not quarters or even years. He has demonstrated this by staying with Alibaba (NYSE: BABA ) for 18 years thus far, or with Yahoo Japan ( OTCPK:YAHOY ) since it was formed. Another size advantage for the Vision Fund has to do with competing VCs and whom they decide to back up. If Masa is behind a specific company, other VCs will think twice before backing up the competitors. Power of the ecosystem. SoftBank has investments in some 1,400 companies, many smaller, but some quite large. Masa discusses this a lot as part of his strategy and vision, as these companies and their leaders/entrepreneurs are a never-ending stream of connections, know how, potential markets/customers, cost-sharing arrangements, etc. He considers this networking ecosystem a critical part of his strategy and personally hosts dinners every few months in the US and Japan with the CEOs that SoftBank invested with. His size allows him to take stakes even in companies that may not need his money and thus he is able to play a King Maker. When he chooses a company in an area he is interested in, he convinces them to let him take a large stake. Usually, the company he chooses is the leader in that area. If they say they don't need his money, he asks them to reconsider by threatening to put money in their biggest competitor. For example, he did that with Chinese ride-hailing service Didi Chuxing ( DIDI ) as well with Uber ( UBER ). If either of those said no to him, he would have considered putting his money into Didi's competitors or in Lyft ( LYFT ). Companies, in general, don't like to face the fact that their biggest competitor is suddenly flush with cash and ready to fight, so they just take the money. There is a sense that VCs and PE funds competing with the Vision Fund have a problem with Masa using the size of his checkbook as a weapon. But there is also a benefit to this approach because it limits the number of competitors who would otherwise create a more fragmented market, without economies of scale. Because of its size and above-mentioned advantages, SoftBank should be able to get better deal terms when it invests . For example, SoftBank's latest Uber round was done at a $48b valuation. At the time previous investor came into Uber, the company was valued at $68b. Thus, SoftBank got a 30% discount when it provided Uber with capital. I'm mentioning Uber in the Vision Fund section although Uber is still being held outside of the Vision Fund and within SoftBank instead. As seemingly unrelated companies find each other under the SoftBank umbrella, there is one thing in common: data. Masa is clearly attempting to use all the data his various holdings collect and then use them across various companies to provide more value to its customers or to crunch it as part of Artificial Intelligence. The Vision Fund Structure Valuing the Vision Fund is like trying to shoot an arrow into a 100 mph moving target. But we can still break it down to some understandable variables. First, SoftBank is both a Limited Partner that owns 1/3 of the fund equity and also the General Partner that charges management and performance fees.
Outside investors cannot buy into simple equity. Rather, for every dollar they invest, 62% is in preferred units that carry 7% interest rate, while the remaining 38% is in equity. So, for example, if Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) invested $1b, they will expect to get paid 7% on $620m with no real upside on that amount, while the $380m is a pure equity with upside.
To be precise, there are actually two funds, SoftBank Vision Fund and Delta Fund, as detailed on page 23 of SoftBank's Sept. 30, 2018, Consolidated Financial Report . Delta Fund is a special carve out financial vehicle created to invest in the Chinese ride-sharing company Didi and avoid conflict for its Saudi Arabian investors who already had their own separate investment in Uber, which is Didi's competitor. In a sense, Saudis didn't want to fund Uber's competitor, and Masa wanted a piece of Didi, so Delta Fund was created to keep Saudis money out of that particular investment.
Once all of committed capital is deployed, here is how it would look like: $97.7b - $32.5b SoftBank stake = $65.2b from outside investors. $65.2b * 62% = $40.4b preferred, with the remaining $24.8b equity that outsider investors own. Thus, at 7% rate, on $40.4b preferreds, the Vision Fund is expected to pay $2.8b in yearly dividends to its outside investors. If Masa is right and he hits some home runs, SoftBank would get disproportionately more upside because all of its stakes is equity. Also, as a manager of the fund, SoftBank gets a fee between 0.7% and 1.3%. If the returns are greater than 8%, SoftBank gets private equity-like 20% of the profits.
Thus far, as of September 30, 2018, actual invested capital from the outside investors is $18b. At 62%, that means preferreds are $11b, so dividends on those are some $800m. Obviously, this number changes as more capital is moved from committed to invested. Once all the committed capital is invested, the Vision Fund clearly needs to produce some minimum cash every year (from my above calculations, that's something close to $2.8b in dividends minus the roughly 1% asset fee, which is $650m, so roughly $2.2b per year).
Valuation It is clear that the Vision Fund is unlike anything else out there. Let's summarize the big picture:
Set up as a private equity, with a significant portion ($40b) to be financed by the preferred shares Its investments are venture capital like late-stage private companies focused on rapid growth and internal reinvestment of their cash flows Fund size and extended lifetime reduce the need for a quick IPO as an exit strategy for its investments Masa's Singularity vision and long-term objectives result in investments that are often designed to position the pieces on the chess board, rather than placate Wall Street's next quarter analysis Holdings are mostly private companies whose valuations may vary greatly and also face a higher risk of failure So, how do we value all of the above? If we simply try to mimic how private equity companies such as KKR, Blackstone, or Carlyle, are valued, that does not quite fit. Venture capital firms also don't come close to how we should look at the Vision Fund.
Instead, I like to think about the Vision Fund simply as a financing vehicle for Masa to make bets on the next technological revolution. This financial structure is not cheap though. Allow me to illustrate with an example. Let's say you are a person with some notable successes in buying businesses and decide to raise $1m from a bank in order to parlay that money into purchasing more business opportunities. But rather than loaning you $1m, the bank says that instead, you have to come up with a $325k equity from the other businesses you already own, then the bank lends you $400k at 7%, and gives you the remaining $275k to be the Bank's equity stake. Essentially, the bank is now almost your equal partner and not only you have to pay interest, but you just gave up equity in other businesses that are expected to be worth more in the future.
Add some more zeros to above numbers, and instead of bank, call it Middle East sovereign funds, and you get to the same conclusion that this is not a cheap financing setup for SoftBank. However, there are some positives as well.
My understanding is that this hybrid structure partly financed by the preferred debt is unusual for a PE or VC type of vehicle. But if you think about it, this also demonstrates that Masa likely killed two birds with one stone by setting up this structure. He could have tried to raise $25b of pure equity, and then go to the banks to borrow another $40b, which could have possibly run into roadblocks because of the other debt on SoftBank's consolidated balance sheet. But this way, his investors get a better risk structure, they effectively loan majority of the money to Masa and get paid to wait while he invests for them, and also through the equity stake they share the upside if things turn out well.
If there is a massive failure, SoftBank loses $32b, and reputation, but not everything. In a sense, and I realize I'm making a very loose comparison here, this is not unlike Berkshire's (NYSE: BRK.A ) (NYSE: BRK.B ) float. Buffett's float allows him access to tremendous amount of capital at a negative interest rate. In turn, Buffett's genius allocates that capital into stable enterprises, mostly low risk, and with decades of success. Masa's float is the Vision Fund. His cost is a lot more than zero or negative cost because Masa is investing in inherently riskier enterprises.
As described above, SoftBank has a dual role in the Vision Fund:
As a general partner/manager, SoftBank will charge an annual 0.7% to 1.3% asset fee, plus the additional 20% of the profits over 8%. As a limited partner/investor, SoftBank gets roughly 55% of the equity, and outside investors get 45% equity stake after the preferreds are subtracted. SoftBank will be entitled to booking gains resulting from increasing valuations, IPO or other types of exit events, and cash flow/dividends if any. Just for the sake of rough estimation, I put together a spreadsheet and attempted to calculate the Vision and Delta Funds Net Present Value for its 14-year life. I made a number of assumptions in my calculations but attempted to stay conservative with them. Here they are:
Based on the latest disclosure from SoftBank's Sept. 30, 2018, Consolidated Financial Report , Vision Fund investments have a fair value of $35.8b, while Delta Fund's fair value is $5b, for a total of $40.8b in current valuation Total investments that arrived to that $41b were $28.9b contributed thus far. $10.9b came from SoftBank and $18b from the outside investors. The $18b is then divided in $11.2b in preferreds (62%), and $6.8 in equity. There is around $66.3b left to deploy, I am assuming that each year, for the next 3 years, $22.1b will be deployed, and by year 4 all $66.3b will be exhausted for deployments I am giving Masa a very pedestrian 10% yearly rate of return to keep this exercise on the conservative side. Sure, Masa's history supports a much higher rate of return, but also he never dealt with this much capital, which if it continues to increase, at some point may be too large relative to the effective deployment opportunities. After 14 years, the fund's total value should be more than $330b. At 10% discount rate, my rough estimate for SoftBank's portion of the Vision Fund's value comes to about $88b in today's dollars. Saudi Arabian government has a significant stake in the Vision Fund, to the tune of $45b committed. Although Saudi Kingdom's current rulers are attempting to conduct a number of reforms in the country, internationally, there have been some developments counterproductive to the Saudi efforts to open up and attract foreign investment or do business internationally. For example:
Detaining a number of Saudi businessmen and placing them under house arrest in the Riyadh Ritz Carlton Hotel. Incident with Canada that followed after Canada raised questions about Saudi treatment of certain human rights activists. Saudi government abruptly cut off all economic ties with Canada, expelled Canadian ambassador, stopped direct flights, but more importantly, it ordered its fund managers to immediately sell any Canadian bond or equity holdings. Finally, and the most concerning, the recent accusations that Saudi government may have been connected to the detaining and possibly killing of a journalist critic while he was visiting Saudi's consulate in Turkey. There are three implications to the above:
Masa, who has been on excellent terms with his biggest investor, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman, may damage his own image if public opinion continues to turn against the Saudis. Masa often appeared in media reports with the Crown Prince. Masa attends and speaks in Saudi organized investment forums and events. He clearly sees not just Saudi money, but their market as well as that of Middle East as an opportunity. Aside from Masa's public reputation, his ability to court the best and brightest young entrepreneurs may also suffer. If the public outcry is loud enough, those entrepreneurs may decide that it is against their long-term interest to be associated with the Saudi capital. This may limit Masa's access to the best investment opportunities. Saudis may decide to change terms, withdraw their committed but not invested capital, or even demand its investment back, as their actions may not be predictable. There are also a number of business ties that SoftBank ventures are developing in Saudi Arabia that could suffer if Saudi's relationship with international community deteriorates. In my opinion, although this political and reputation risk is clearly there, considering that Saudi Arabia plays an important ally for the Western interests in the Middle East and is more often on the same side as the US, I believe that the risk of sanctions or major international condemnation that changes the balance of power in the Saudi Kingdom is likely low. It probably doesn't hurt that the Saudis have significant funds to invest and that their markets are opening up.
However, if I am wrong, and suddenly Saudi Arabia's backed investments are not palatable to the progressive owners of young Silicon Valley startups, Masa may struggle to fill the $45b (or $60b if UAE takes Saudi side) gap if he has to distance himself from the Saudis. But certainly, there are options, although it is anyone's guess how things could play through. I found this CNBC article that does a decent job of discussing some options if there is a fallout. Probably the most palatable impact of recent events has been Masa's cancellation of appearance at a so-called Davos at the Desert, which was in line with a number of CEOs and leading business figures.
WeWork Last year, the Vision Fund invested $4.4b in a shared space startup WeWork, gaining 2 board seats and some 20% of the equity at the then $20b WeWork valuation. There have been recent media reports, such as this Wall Street Journal article that speculated the Vision Fund is about to put another $15b to $20b to take majority stake in WeWork. If this transaction takes place, overall concern is that Masa would be putting a significant portion of the Vision Fund into one company. Although WeWork is innovative in its approach to office space, it is difficult to see what moat WeWork has, as it appears relatively straightforward for the competitors to jump in and provide the same service. Additionally, commercial real estate is notoriously cyclical, and although office space is in high demand currently, during the downturn, tenants will look to cut costs, consolidate space, or even go out of business, all resulting in a significant risk to a company such as WeWork which takes long-term leases and then provides short-term arrangements for its tenants.
I tend to agree with the economic risk of this business and am not personally convinced that the Vision Fund should bet the farm on WeWork. From my understanding of Masa's overall approach, he is always looking for synergies and touchpoints where entrepreneurs or the companies he has stakes in can collaborate. In his presentations, he discussed using AI in shared workspace setting that can improve communication and productivity. He also mentioned that one WeWork rented desk brings in 10 times more revenue than one mobile user as compared to his SoftBank Mobile or Sprint holdings. Also, SoftBank has been active in setting up separate partnerships with WeWork in Japan and other Asian countries that give SoftBank more ownership and control. Owning majority of WeWork would allow him to speed this up and drive it more, but I still get a sense that he could do the same even as a current 20% owner. And again, in the optimistic scenario with economy on a tear, WeWork story may be a winner. But what happens when things slow down, will WeWork still be able to thrive or survive?
However, if you study Masa, you will notice that he does not necessarily reveal all the cards to the public on the companies he purchases. Good example is ARM, where he figured that he needed to make the move and acquire ARM to be the central nervous system of his Singularity strategy. But he didn't necessarily leave all that in the open while negotiating because he was concerned that someone else may swoop in and take it from under his nose. Also, as discussed in Parts I and II of this analysis, Masa likes to make many moves in advance, and the full puzzle is not readily available at the time he makes the move.
Masa's critics would say that he is just a man with a huge checkbook, making hasty decisions which will result in a spectacular value destruction one day. Certainly, those critics should be paid attention to when considering investing with Masa. One of the purposes of this write-up is to expose Masa's philosophy and the way he does things.
Personally, I prefer to step back and look at both the history and the big picture, rather than fret over every decision Masa makes. Admittedly, there are a lot of distortions and media slants, mixed with high complexity and lots of moving parts with Masa, SoftBank, and the Vision Fund. All this creates lots of noise and distorts the big picture. Media scrutiny and second-guessing will always be there. I am accepting the fact that Masa will make mistakes, some of them probably spectacular, considering the size of the capital involved. But my bet is that his contributions will outweigh the mistakes, resulting in growing SoftBank's intrinsic value over a long period of time.
Holdings Valuations The tricky part of the Vision Fund valuation is that most of its holdings are privately owned companies, not yet available on the public exchanges. So to value them, we can use the latest capital raising rounds as a benchmark. In a healthy economy, as more capital finds its way to these enterprises, their valuations are bound to grow. And just as the values of publicly traded companies are likely to decline in a recessionary type environment, we can expect that private companies' valuations will react the same. This is another risk that an investor should be aware of when investing with Masa.
To counterbalance some of the above concerns, we should highlight some of the successes thus far with the Vision Fund. For example, earlier this year, the Vision Fund sold its 20% stake in Indian Flipkart to Walmart (NYSE: WMT ) after Walmart decided to purchase the entire company for $16b, netting the Vision Fund $4b on a $2.5b investment.
Other Investments: $18.85b Although all the attention is on the $100b Vision Fund, there is another group of very valuable assets still wholly owned by SoftBank instead of the Vision Fund. The company has been discussing that some of these will eventually move into the Vision Fund, probably to satisfy SoftBank's contribution requirements, similar to how ARM's 25% ownership was used for that purpose. But for now, these holdings are outside of the Vision Fund and they deserve a valuation discussion. The table below lists these assets.

Grab Ride Sharing $3.85b 60% Will Grab & Uber merge, with SoftBank now a shareholder of both? - TLD by MW GM Cruise Autonomous Driving $2.25b 20% Briefing: SoftBank Invests $2.25 Billion in GM's Cruise DoorDash Food Delivery $0.5b 38% DoorDash is raising $535 million from SoftBank and others at a $1.4 billion valuation Total $18.85b Aside from the valuations, it is interesting to see SoftBank's heft in the ride-hailing business worldwide. Masa's strategy is to hold stakes in leaders that operate in multiple countries and then consolidate where it makes sense, as this Forbes article describes. Another article does a great job explaining how SoftBank plays a puppet master and eliminates unhealthy competition while leaving one dominant and likely economically viable company to rule that market.
In terms of valuations, I am counting the cost of these investments, and they add up to around $18.85b. Once some of these companies go public, it is quite possible these stakes will be worth multiples of what Masa paid for them. For example, there have been recent media reports that investment bankers are potentially valuing Uber at $120b ahead of its IPO. If that turns out to be accurate, Masa's $9.25b, 15% stake, would be worth $18b to SoftBank.
This concludes Part III. In Part IV, I will discuss SoftBank's debt, risk, and put it all together in terms of valuation
